name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_COORDINATIONCOMPOUNDS_DIAGRAM_Q01 - Denticity and donor atoms of EDTA ligand

questiontext.text: Identify the denticity and the exact donor atoms of the ligand shown in the structural diagram below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows the structural formula of the ethylenediaminetetraacetate ion (\(\mathrm{EDTA^{4-}}\)), consisting of an ethane-1,2-diamine backbone (\(\mathrm{-CH_2-CH_2-}\)) attached to two nitrogen atoms, with each nitrogen atom bearing two \(\mathrm{-CH_2COO^-}\) (acetate) groups.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Denticity is defined as the number of ligating (donor) atoms in a single ligand that can simultaneously coordinate to a central metal ion.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Each tertiary amine nitrogen atom possesses one lone pair of electrons, and each carboxylate group (\(\mathrm{-COO^-}\)) provides one negatively charged donor oxygen atom for coordination.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Counting the donor sites in the structure: there are \(2\) nitrogen atoms (each contributing \(1\) donor site) and \(4\) \(\mathrm{-CH_2COO^-}\) groups (each contributing \(1\) oxygen donor site). Thus, the total number of donor atoms is \(2 + 4 = 6\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Therefore, \(\mathrm{EDTA^{4-}}\) is a hexadentate ligand that binds to a central metal ion through two nitrogen atoms and four oxygen atoms.

answer.text: Hexadentate; two nitrogen atoms and four oxygen atoms
Hexadentate; four nitrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_COORDINATIONCOMPOUNDS_DIAGRAM_Q02 - Identification of square planar coordination polyhedron

questiontext.text: Which of the following coordination entities adopts the coordination polyhedron shown in the diagram below (where \(\mathrm{M}\) is the central atom/ion and \(\mathrm{L}\) is a unidentate ligand)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram depicts a square planar coordination polyhedron with a central metal \(\mathrm{M}\) bonded to four unidentate ligands \(\mathrm{L}\) in a single plane at \(90^\circ\) angles.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The coordination number of \(\mathrm{M}\) in this polyhedron is \(4\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Different complexes have characteristic geometries: \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\) is tetrahedral, \(\mathrm{[PtCl_4]^{2-}}\) is square planar, \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) is octahedral, and \(\mathrm{[Fe(CO)_5]}\) is trigonal bipyramidal.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Comparing the coordination numbers and geometries: \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) has coordination number \(6\) (octahedral) and \(\mathrm{[Fe(CO)_5]}\) has coordination number \(5\) (trigonal bipyramidal). Both \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\) and \(\mathrm{[PtCl_4]^{2-}}\) have coordination number \(4\), but \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\) is tetrahedral (\(sp^3\)) whereas \(\mathrm{[PtCl_4]^{2-}}\) is square planar (\(dsp^2\)).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Thus, \(\mathrm{[PtCl_4]^{2-}}\) adopts the square planar coordination polyhedron shown in the diagram.

questiontext.text: Which type of isomerism and specific isomer is represented by the octahedral structure of \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_3(NO_2)_3]}\) shown in the diagram below?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows an octahedral \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_3(NO_2)_3]}\) complex where three \(\mathrm{NO_2^-}\) ligands occupy three adjacent positions forming one triangular face of the octahedron (highlighted in red), while the three \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) ligands occupy the opposite triangular face.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Octahedral complexes of the type \(\mathrm{[Ma_3b_3]}\) exhibit geometrical isomerism in two forms: facial (fac-) and meridional (mer-).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
When three identical donor atoms occupy adjacent positions at the corners of one octahedral face, the isomer is called the facial (fac-) isomer. When three identical ligands occupy positions around the meridian of the octahedron (with two of them trans to each other), it is called the meridional (mer-) isomer.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
In the given structure, all three \(\mathrm{NO_2^-}\) ligands are mutually cis (\(90^\circ\) apart) and lie on the same triangular face of the octahedron, and all three \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) ligands lie on the opposite triangular face.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Therefore, the diagram represents the facial (fac-) geometrical isomer of \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_3(NO_2)_3]}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_COORDINATIONCOMPOUNDS_DIAGRAM_Q04 - Geometrical isomerism in square planar platinum complex

questiontext.text: Which statement correctly describes the coordination entity \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]}\) depicted in the diagram below?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows a planar four-coordinate \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]}\) complex in which the two \(\mathrm{Cl}\) ligands are positioned diagonally opposite (\(180^\circ\)) to each other, and the two \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) ligands are also diagonally opposite to each other.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In a square planar complex of formula \(\mathrm{[MX_2L_2]}\), identical ligands arranged adjacent (\(90^\circ\)) form the cis-isomer, whereas identical ligands arranged opposite (\(180^\circ\)) form the trans-isomer.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Square planar complexes possess a molecular plane of symmetry (the plane containing the central metal and all four donor atoms), which makes them superimposable on their mirror images and hence optically inactive.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Because the two \(\mathrm{Cl}\) ligands lie opposite one another and the two \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) ligands lie opposite one another, the structure is the trans-isomer. Being square planar, it has a plane of symmetry and does not show optical isomerism.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Thus, the depicted complex is the trans-isomer with square planar geometry and is optically inactive.

answer.text: It is the cis-isomer and exhibits optical activity.
It is the cis-isomer with a tetrahedral geometry.
It is the trans-isomer and shows optical isomerism.
It is the trans-isomer with square planar geometry and is optically inactive.

questiontext.text: What relationship exists between the two coordination entities of \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3+}}\) shown across the mirror plane in the diagram below?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows two mirror-image octahedral structures of \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3+}}\) separated by a mirror plane, labelled dextro and laevo.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3+}}\), three identical bidentate ethane-1,2-diamine (\(\mathrm{en}\)) ligands chelate the central \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) ion in a propeller-like chiral arrangement.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Chiral molecules or ions that are non-superimposable mirror images of one another are called enantiomers (optical isomers). The dextro (\(d\)) form rotates plane-polarised light to the right, while the laevo (\(l\)) form rotates it to the left.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Because \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3+}}\) lacks any plane or centre of symmetry, the two mirror-image forms cannot be superimposed on each other. They are distinct optical isomers.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Thus, the two structures are enantiomers (optical isomers) that rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions.

answer.text: They are enantiomers (optical isomers) that rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions.
They are linkage isomers differing in donor atoms.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_COORDINATIONCOMPOUNDS_DIAGRAM_Q06 - Valence bond orbital diagram of hexaamminecobalt(III)

questiontext.text: Based on the Valence Bond Theory orbital diagram shown below for \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\), what are the magnetic behaviour and complex classification?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The orbital diagram of \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) shows three \(3d\) orbitals completely filled with paired electrons (`↑↓ ↑↓ ↑↓`) and six \(d^2sp^3\) hybrid orbitals (formed from two inner \(3d\), one \(4s\), and three \(4p\) orbitals) occupied by six electron pairs donated by six \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) ligands.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In Valence Bond Theory, a complex is diamagnetic if it contains no unpaired electrons and paramagnetic if it contains one or more unpaired electrons. Complexes using inner \((n-1)d\) orbitals for hybridisation are called inner orbital (or low spin / spin paired) complexes.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) has a \(3d^6\) configuration. Pairing of all six \(3d\) electrons into three \(3d\) orbitals vacates two \(3d\) orbitals for \(d^2sp^3\) hybridisation.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since all electrons in the \(3d\) orbitals and in the \(d^2sp^3\) hybrid orbitals are paired, the number of unpaired electrons is \(n = 0\), making the complex diamagnetic. Because the inner \(3d\) orbitals are used in hybridisation, it is classified as an inner orbital (low spin) complex.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Therefore, \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) is diamagnetic and is an inner orbital (low spin) complex.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_COORDINATIONCOMPOUNDS_DIAGRAM_Q07 - Geometry and magnetic moment of tetrachloridonickelate(II)

questiontext.text: From the Valence Bond Theory orbital diagram of \(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}\) shown below, determine the geometry and spin-only magnetic moment (in BM) of the complex ion.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The orbital diagram of \(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}\) shows five \(3d\) orbitals containing eight electrons (`↑↓ ↑↓ ↑↓ ↑ ↑`), leaving \(n = 2\) unpaired electrons, and four \(sp^3\) hybrid orbitals filled with four pairs of electrons from four \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) ligands.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The geometry of a complex is determined by its hybridisation, and the spin-only magnetic moment \(\mu\) is calculated in Bohr Magnetons (BM) from the number of unpaired electrons \(n\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(sp^3\) hybridisation corresponds to a tetrahedral geometry. The spin-only magnetic moment formula is: \[\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\text{ BM}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substituting \(n = 2\) unpaired electrons into the magnetic moment formula: \[\mu = \sqrt{2(2+2)} = \sqrt{8} \approx 2.83\text{ BM}\] Because the hybridisation is \(sp^3\), the geometry is tetrahedral.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking units and magnitude, \(\sqrt{8}\text{ BM} \approx 2.83\text{ BM}\) is consistent with two unpaired electrons. Thus, \(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}\) has a tetrahedral geometry and a spin-only magnetic moment of \(2.83\text{ BM}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_COORDINATIONCOMPOUNDS_DIAGRAM_Q08 - Crystal field stabilisation energy for high-spin d4 ion

questiontext.text: Using the octahedral crystal field splitting diagram shown below, what is the crystal field stabilisation energy (CFSE) for a high-spin \(d^4\) metal ion (where \(\Delta_o < P\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows the octahedral crystal field splitting of five \(d\) orbitals into a lower-energy triply degenerate \(t_{2g}\) set at \(-\frac{2}{5}\Delta_o\) and a higher-energy doubly degenerate \(e_g\) set at \(+\frac{3}{5}\Delta_o\) relative to the barycentre. We are considering a high-spin \(d^4\) ion with \(\Delta_o < P\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Energies below the barycentre are negative (\(-\frac{2}{5}\Delta_o = -0.4\Delta_o\) per \(t_{2g}\) electron), and energies above the barycentre are positive (\(+\frac{3}{5}\Delta_o = +0.6\Delta_o\) per \(e_g\) electron).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
When \(\Delta_o < P\), the fourth electron enters an \(e_g\) orbital rather than pairing in \(t_{2g}\), giving the electronic configuration \(t_{2g}^3 e_g^1\). The CFSE is given by: \[\text{CFSE} = n_{t_{2g}}\left(-\frac{2}{5}\Delta_o\right) + n_{e_g}\left(+\frac{3}{5}\Delta_o\right)\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substituting \(n_{t_{2g}} = 3\) and \(n_{e_g} = 1\): \[\text{CFSE} = 3\left(-0.4\Delta_o\right) + 1\left(+0.6\Delta_o\right) = -1.2\Delta_o + 0.6\Delta_o = -0.6\Delta_o\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \(-0.6\Delta_o = -\frac{3}{5}\Delta_o\), the net stabilisation is negative relative to the spherical field. Thus, the CFSE for a high-spin \(d^4\) ion is \(-0.6\Delta_o\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_COORDINATIONCOMPOUNDS_DIAGRAM_Q09 - Tetrahedral crystal field splitting and symmetry notation

questiontext.text: Based on the tetrahedral crystal field splitting diagram shown below, which statement is correct regarding the energy levels and electronic configuration of a tetrahedral complex?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows the crystal field splitting of \(d\) orbitals in a tetrahedral field: the \(t_2\) orbitals (\(d_{xy}, d_{yz}, d_{xz}\)) are raised in energy by \(\frac{2}{5}\Delta_t\) above the barycentre, while the \(e\) orbitals (\(d_{x^2-y^2}, d_{z^2}\)) are lowered by \(\frac{3}{5}\Delta_t\) below the barycentre.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Tetrahedral splitting is inverted relative to octahedral splitting, and \(\Delta_t = \frac{4}{9}\Delta_o\) for the same metal, ligands, and metal-ligand distances.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The 'g' (gerade) subscript is used only for geometries possessing a centre of symmetry, such as octahedral and square planar complexes. Because a tetrahedron lacks a centre of symmetry, 'g' is omitted from \(t_2\) and \(e\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Comparing the levels in the diagram, the \(t_2\) set (\(d_{xy}, d_{yz}, d_{xz}\)) lies higher in energy than the \(e\) set (\(d_{x^2-y^2}, d_{z^2}\)). Furthermore, since \(\Delta_t = \frac{4}{9}\Delta_o\) is small, \(\Delta_t < P\) and low-spin configurations are rarely observed in tetrahedral complexes.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Thus, the \(d_{xy}\), \(d_{yz}\), and \(d_{xz}\) orbitals are higher in energy than \(d_{x^2-y^2}\) and \(d_{z^2}\), and the 'g' subscript is omitted because tetrahedral complexes lack a centre of symmetry.

answer.text: The \(d_{xy}\), \(d_{yz}\), and \(d_{xz}\) orbitals are higher in energy than \(d_{x^2-y^2}\) and \(d_{z^2}\) orbitals, and the 'g' subscript is omitted because tetrahedral complexes lack a centre of symmetry.
The \(d_{x^2-y^2}\) and \(d_{z^2}\) orbitals are higher in energy than \(d_{xy}\), \(d_{yz}\), and \(d_{xz}\) orbitals, and low-spin configurations are commonly observed.
The splitting energy \(\Delta_t\) is greater than \(\Delta_o\) for the same metal and ligands, so \(\Delta_t = \frac{9}{4}\Delta_o\).
The 'g' subscript is omitted because tetrahedral complexes are always diamagnetic.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_COORDINATIONCOMPOUNDS_DIAGRAM_Q10 - d-d electronic transition and colour in hexaaquatitanium(III)

questiontext.text: The diagram below illustrates the \(d\text{--}d\) electronic transition in \(\mathrm{[Ti(H_2O)_6]^{3+}}\) upon absorbing light at \(498\text{ nm}\) (blue-green region). What is the observed colour of the complex, and why does anhydrous \(\mathrm{TiCl_3}\) (obtained on heating \(\mathrm{[Ti(H_2O)_6]Cl_3}\)) become colourless?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows the single \(3d^1\) electron of \(\mathrm{Ti^{3+}}\) in \(\mathrm{[Ti(H_2O)_6]^{3+}}\) being excited from the \(t_{2g}\) level (ground state \(t_{2g}^1 e_g^0\)) to the \(e_g\) level (excited state \(t_{2g}^0 e_g^1\)) upon absorbing a photon \(h\nu\) at \(498\text{ nm}\) (blue-green region).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The observed colour of a coordination complex is complementary to the colour of the visible light absorbed.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
According to Crystal Field Theory, crystal field splitting (\(\Delta_o\)) occurs only when ligands surround the central metal ion. In the absence of ligands, the five \(d\) orbitals remain degenerate, so no \(d\text{--}d\) transition can occur.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since \(\mathrm{[Ti(H_2O)_6]^{3+}}\) absorbs blue-green light (\(498\text{ nm}\)), the transmitted complementary colour observed is violet. When \(\mathrm{[Ti(H_2O)_6]Cl_3}\) is heated to remove water ligands, crystal field splitting disappears, preventing \(d\text{--}d\) transitions and rendering the anhydrous salt colourless.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Thus, the complex appears violet, and anhydrous \(\mathrm{TiCl_3}\) is colourless because crystal field splitting does not occur in the absence of ligands.

answer.text: Violet; in the absence of ligands, crystal field splitting does not occur, so no \(d\text{--}d\) transition takes place.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_COORDINATIONCOMPOUNDS_DIAGRAM_Q11 - Synergic bonding interactions in metal carbonyls

questiontext.text: Which statement accurately interprets the synergic bonding interactions depicted in the metal carbonyl diagram below?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows a metal atom \(\mathrm{M}\) bonded to a carbon monoxide (\(\mathrm{CO}\)) ligand via two complementary electron-donation pathways: a \(\sigma\) interaction directed from \(\mathrm{C}\) to \(\mathrm{M}\), and \(\pi\) interactions directed from filled \(d\) orbitals of \(\mathrm{M}\) into vacant \(\pi^*\) orbitals of \(\mathrm{CO}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In metal carbonyls, the \(\mathrm{M\text{--}C}\) bond possesses both \(\sigma\) and \(\pi\) character, creating a synergic effect that strengthens the \(\mathrm{M\text{--}CO}\) bond.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The \(\mathrm{M\text{--}C}\) \(\sigma\) bond is formed by donation of the lone pair of electrons on the carbonyl carbon into a vacant orbital of the metal. The \(\mathrm{M\text{--}C}\) \(\pi\) bond is formed by donation of a pair of electrons from a filled \(d\) orbital of the metal into the vacant antibonding \(\pi^*\) orbital of carbon monoxide.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
This mutual reinforcement—\(\sigma\) donation from \(\mathrm{CO}\) to \(\mathrm{M}\) accompanied by \(\pi\) back-donation from \(\mathrm{M}\) to \(\mathrm{CO}\)—strengthens the overall \(\mathrm{M\text{--}C}\) bond.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Thus, the \(\mathrm{M\text{--}C}\) \(\sigma\) bond is formed by donation of a carbon lone pair into a vacant metal orbital, while the \(\mathrm{M\text{--}C}\) \(\pi\) bond is formed by back-donation from a filled metal \(d\) orbital into the vacant \(\pi^*\) orbital of \(\mathrm{CO}\).

answer.text: Both \(\sigma\) and \(\pi\) bonds are formed by electron-pair donation from carbon monoxide to the vacant metal \(d\) orbitals.
The \(\mathrm{M\text{--}C}\) \(\sigma\) bond involves donation from a filled metal \(d\) orbital to \(\mathrm{CO}\), while the \(\pi\) bond involves donation from \(\mathrm{CO}\) to the metal.

The \(\mathrm{M\text{--}C}\) \(\sigma\) bond is formed by donation of a carbon lone pair into a vacant metal orbital, while the \(\mathrm{M\text{--}C}\) \(\pi\) bond is formed by back-donation from a filled metal \(d\) orbital into the vacant \(\pi^*\) orbital of \(\mathrm{CO}\).
The back-donation into the \(\pi^*\) orbital of \(\mathrm{CO}\) weakens both the \(\mathrm{C\text{--}O}\) bond and the \(\mathrm{M\text{--}C}\) bond.
